intro: Every country has to answer a hard question. Who gets to make the rules? In some places a king or queen decides. In others, voters choose leaders and can replace them. In still others, one person or one party holds power and no one can vote them out.

People also argue about what the rules should be. For more than 200 years, they have used two words to sort those arguments: left and right. These words began with where lawmakers sat in a French hall in 1789. Today you hear them on the news almost every day, in many countries.

In this unit you will learn where left and right came from and what they usually mean. You will compare monarchy, democracy and dictatorship. By the end, you will be able to spot the signs of a free and fair election and explain ideas from different sides fairly.
bigQuestion: How do people decide who holds power, and how can citizens tell whether that power is fair and limited?

timeline.t: Athens begins one of the first democracies
Louis XIV becomes king of France and later rules as an absolute monarch
The English Bill of Rights limits the monarch's power
James Madison explains checks and balances in The Federalist No. 51
France's Third Estate forms a National Assembly; seating creates 'left' and 'right'
Edmund Burke warns that the French Revolution is moving too fast
The United Nations adopts the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
Mao Zedong begins ruling China as a one-party state
A military coup overthrows Chile's elected president
Chile returns to democracy after voters reject Pinochet

the side of politics that usually stresses equality and change

test.q: In 1789, supporters of the king in the National Assembly sat
choices: to the right of the president
to the left of the president
test.why: Supporters of the king and tradition gathered to the right, which gave us the political 'right.'

test.q: Which idea does the left usually stress?
test.why: The left usually stresses equality and openness to change.

test.q: Which idea does the right usually stress?
choices: Tradition, order and liberty from government
test.why: The right usually stresses tradition and order, and often liberty from government.

test.q: Why must you know the place and time before deciding what 'right' means?
choices: The word is only used in France
It always means the same thing
Its meaning differs by country and era
test.why: Left and right are relative words that shift by place and time.

test.q: What is the main limit of the one-line political spectrum?
choices: Many people's views do not fit one spot
test.why: A model leaves things out, and real people mix views.

choices: Voters choose the head of state
One monarch holds nearly all power
test.why: In an absolute monarchy, like Louis XIV's France, the monarch holds nearly all power.
The UK has a king, but elected lawmakers make the laws.
Mexico's head of state is elected, so it is a republic.

test.q: How is direct democracy different from representative democracy?
choices: In direct democracy citizens vote on laws themselves
test.why: In direct democracy citizens decide laws; in representative democracy they elect lawmakers.

test.q: Which branch of the U.S. government decides what laws mean?
test.why: The judicial branch, the courts, decides what laws mean.

test.q: Madison's line 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition' supports
test.why: Madison argued that power should be set against power, the core of checks and balances.

test.q: Which is a sign of a free and fair election?
choices: Only one name on the ballot
The press may not criticize the leader
The losing leader hands over power peacefully
test.why: A peaceful handover after a loss is one of the clearest signs of a fair election.

choices: A country where only one party may hold power
A country with two strong parties
A country ruled by a monarch
test.why: In a one-party state, other parties are banned or powerless.

test.q: Which pair were dictators of the far left?
test.why: Stalin and Mao led Communist governments on the far left.

choices: A sudden takeover of government, often by the army
A meeting of the three estates
test.why: A coup is a sudden, forceful takeover, like Chile's in 1973.

write.prompt: Which is the best protection against a leader who abuses power: checks and balances, free and fair elections, or a free press? Make a claim. Support it with two or three facts or sources from this unit, and explain why your choice matters most.
tips: Name your sources, such as Madison's Federalist No. 51 or Article 21 of the Universal Declaration.
Use at least one example from history, like Louis XIV, Chile or a one-party state.
Explain the strongest reason someone might pick a different answer.
Use unit words such as republic, veto, secret ballot and dictator.
